decks.title: Social Responsibility of Business: Concept and Case
goals: Define social responsibility and tell it apart from legal responsibility
Present the arguments for and against social responsibility, as views held by different people
Explain the four kinds of social responsibility and the factors that led firms to accept social obligations
Describe the corporate social responsibility rule of section 135 of the Companies Act 2013, as of 2024, and work out a spend

slides.heading: Social Responsibility of Business: Concept and Case
slides.body_md: Part 1: what social responsibility is, why people argue for and against it, its kinds and the law.

nodes.label: Factors and the law on CSR

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: concept of social responsibility, the case for and against, kinds of responsibility, and the factors and the law on corporate social responsibility as of 2024

slides.narration: A dye factory beside a river must decide how to treat its waste. Obeying the law is one thing. Doing what society values is wider. In this part we define social responsibility, set out the arguments for and against it, study its kinds, and see what the Companies Act asks of large companies.

slides.heading: What is social responsibility?
slides.body_md: **Social responsibility** is the obligation of business to take decisions and actions that are desirable in terms of the objectives and values of society.

rows: The obligation of business to take decisions and actions that are desirable in terms of the objectives and values of society
The duty to comply with the law
Social responsibility goes beyond what the law requires

visual.alt: Table defining social responsibility as the obligation of business to take decisions and actions that are desirable in terms of the objectives and values of society, and legal responsibility as the duty to comply with the law, with social responsibility going beyond the law

slides.narration: Social responsibility is the obligation of business to take decisions and actions that are desirable in terms of the objectives and values of society. Legal responsibility is the duty to comply with the law. Social responsibility is wider, because it goes beyond what the law requires.

slides.heading: Going beyond the law

rows: Installs the wastewater unit that the rules demand, and nothing more
Also funds a clean drinking water tank for the villagers beside the river
Goes beyond the law: social responsibility
Hides the volume of waste in its returns

visual.alt: Table of three imagined acts of Rangrez Dyeworks: meeting only the rules is legal responsibility, funding a water tank for villagers goes beyond the law, and hiding the waste volume fails even the legal duty

slides.narration: Our imagined factory, Rangrez Dyeworks, sets up the wastewater unit that the rules demand. That meets its legal responsibility only. If it also pays for a clean water tank for the villagers, it goes beyond the law. If it hides its waste volume, it fails even the legal duty.

slides.heading: Quick check: is it the same as the law?
slides.body_md: True or false: social responsibility means the same thing as obeying the law.
slides.narration: Think about whether a firm can obey every law and still fall short of what society values.

visual.alt: Chart of the case for and the case against social responsibility. Case for, eight arguments: justification for the existence and growth of business, long-term interest of the firm, avoidance of government regulation, maintenance of society, availability of resources with business, converting problems into opportunities, a better environment for doing business, and responsibility for problems it has caused. Case against, four arguments: violation of the profit-maximisation objective, burden on consumers through higher prices, lack of social skills, and lack of broad public support
visual.caption: Arguments on both sides, as some argue and others argue.

slides.narration: This chart sets out the arguments on both sides. Eight arguments are put in favour, and four against. Remember that each one is a view held by some people. Thoughtful people weigh them differently, and a good answer presents both sides with fairness.

slides.heading: Arguments for, first four

rows: Business exists by the leave of society and serves its needs
A good name and loyal partners help a firm to earn for years
Responsible conduct leaves less reason for strict rules
Business depends on a sound society and gains from keeping it so

visual.alt: Table of four arguments for social responsibility: justification for existence and growth, long-term interest of the firm, avoidance of government regulation, and maintenance of society

slides.narration: Some argue that business exists by the leave of society and serves its needs, which justifies its existence and growth. Some argue that a good name helps the long term interest of the firm. Others argue that responsible conduct avoids government regulation. And some say business depends on a sound society, which is the maintenance of society.

slides.heading: Arguments for, other four

rows: Business holds money, skills and equipment that social work needs
A social problem can open a new line of business
A better environment for doing business
Healthy, educated and safe communities are better places to trade
Responsibility for problems it has caused
A firm that causes harm should help to repair it

visual.alt: Table of four more arguments for social responsibility: availability of resources with business, converting problems into opportunities, a better environment for doing business, and holding business responsible for problems it has caused

slides.narration: Some argue that business holds money, skills and equipment that social work needs. Others say that a social problem can open a new line of business. Some say healthy and safe communities are better places to trade. And some argue that a firm that causes harm should help to repair it.

slides.body_md: Three imagined cases. Find the clue, name the side and the argument.
bullets: Step 1: Read what the speaker says or does.
Step 2: Decide whether it is for or against.
Step 3: Name the argument and give the reason.

rows: Surya Steel Works owns cranes and trucks that a flooded district lacks
For: availability of resources with business
A shareholder says that social spending cuts the profit of the owners
A cement makers association adopts its own dust rules before a law is framed

visual.alt: Worked example table of clues and the argument each points to: owning cranes and trucks that others lack is availability of resources, a shareholder saying that spending cuts owner profit is the profit-maximisation argument against, and adopting dust rules before a law is framed is avoidance of regulation
visual.caption: Find the clue, then name the side and the argument.

slides.narration: Surya Steel Works owns cranes and trucks that a flooded district lacks. That is an argument for, availability of resources. A shareholder says social spending cuts owner profit. That is an argument against, violation of profit maximisation. A makers association adopts its own dust rules before a law is framed. That is avoidance of government regulation.

slides.heading: Arguments against

headers: Meaning, as put by those who hold it
rows: Some argue that a firm exists to earn the most profit for its owners
Burden on consumers through higher prices
Some argue that the cost will be added to prices
Some argue that managers are trained for business, not social work
Some argue that people do not wish business to take up social work

visual.alt: Table of four arguments against social responsibility, each stated as the view of those who hold it: violation of the profit-maximisation objective, burden on consumers through higher prices, lack of social skills, and lack of broad public support

slides.narration: Some argue that a firm exists to earn the most profit for its owners, so social spending violates that aim. Some argue that the cost will be added to prices, a burden on consumers. Some say managers lack social skills. And some say the public does not wish business to take up social work, which is a lack of broad public support.

slides.heading: Quick check: which argument against?
slides.body_md: A shareholder says every rupee spent on a free school is a rupee less for the owners. Name the argument.
slides.narration: Think about whose money the speaker is worried about.

visual.alt: Chart of four kinds of social responsibility. Economic: produce goods and services and earn a fair profit, as the imagined Tarang Appliances does with sound fans. Legal: follow the laws of the land, as the imagined Hariyali Paper Mills does by paying tax and keeping to smoke limits. Ethical: do what is right and fair even where no law compels, as the imagined Amrit Dugdh does by not selling a product it thinks unsafe. Discretionary: give or act by choice, as the imagined Byteloom Software does by lending staff to teach at a village school
visual.caption: Four kinds, from what is needed to what is chosen.

slides.narration: This chart shows four kinds. Economic responsibility is to produce goods and earn a fair profit. Legal responsibility is to follow the law. Ethical responsibility is to do what is right where no law compels. Discretionary responsibility is to give or act by choice, with no law or custom demanding it.

slides.heading: The kinds with imagined examples

rows: Produce goods and services and earn a profit
Tarang Appliances sells sound fans at fair prices
Hariyali Paper Mills pays tax and keeps to smoke limits
Do what is right where no law compels
Amrit Dugdh will not sell a product it thinks unsafe
Byteloom Software lends staff to a village school

visual.alt: Table of four kinds of social responsibility with a meaning and an imagined example of each: economic, legal, ethical including moral, and discretionary or voluntary

slides.narration: Tarang Appliances sells sound fans at fair prices, which is economic. Hariyali Paper Mills pays tax and keeps to smoke limits, which is legal. Amrit Dugdh will not sell a product it thinks unsafe, though no law bans it, which is ethical, including moral responsibility. Byteloom Software lends staff to a village school, which is discretionary, or voluntary.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: classify the kind
slides.body_md: Four imagined acts. Ask whether each is needed, required, right or chosen.
bullets: Step 1: Is it about production and profit? Economic.
Step 2: Is a law behind it? Legal.
Step 3: Is it right with no law behind it? Ethical.
Step 4: Is it a free gift to society? Discretionary.

rows: A bakery earns a profit by selling fresh bread at fair prices
A factory files its returns on time and meets the waste rules
A shop recalls goods that it fears are unsafe, though no rule asks it to
A mill pays for a free health camp in a nearby village by its own choice

visual.alt: Worked example table of clues and the kind each shows: a bakery earning profit with fair prices is economic, filing returns and meeting waste rules is legal, recalling goods that it fears are unsafe with no rule is ethical, and paying for a free health camp by choice is discretionary
visual.caption: Ask whether the act is needed, required, right or chosen.

slides.narration: A bakery earning a profit by selling fresh bread at fair prices is economic. A factory that files returns and meets waste rules is legal. A shop that recalls goods it fears are unsafe, with no rule asking it to, is ethical. A mill that pays for a health camp by its own choice is discretionary.

slides.heading: Factors behind the acceptance of social obligations

rows: Firms act first to keep the government from framing strict rules
Organised workers press for fair treatment
Aware buyers expect honest goods and dealing
Society expects fair and honest conduct
Courses teach the duties of business to society
Relationship between social interest and business interest
Firms see that the two often move together
Development of a professional managerial class
Trained managers weigh society as well as owners

visual.alt: Table of seven factors that influenced the acceptance of social obligations: threat of public regulation, pressure of the labour movement, impact of consumer consciousness, development of social standards, development of business education, the relationship between social interest and business interest, and the development of a professional managerial class

slides.narration: Seven factors moved firms to accept social obligations. The threat of public regulation. The pressure of the labour movement. The impact of consumer consciousness. The development of social standards. The development of business education. The relationship between social interest and business interest. And the development of a professional managerial class.

slides.heading: The law on corporate social responsibility, as of 2024

rows: A company with a net worth of Rs 500 crore or more, or a turnover of Rs 1,000 crore or more, or a net profit of Rs 5 crore or more
At least 2 per cent of the average net profits of the three preceding years
Limits and rules change by amendment; check the present position

visual.alt: Table of the corporate social responsibility rule as of 2024: a company with a net worth of 500 crore rupees or more, or a turnover of 1,000 crore rupees or more, or a net profit of 5 crore rupees or more must spend at least 2 per cent of the average net profits of the three preceding years on social responsibility activities, with a note that limits can change

slides.narration: As of two thousand twenty four, section one hundred thirty five of the Companies Act two thousand thirteen covers a company with a net worth of five hundred crore rupees or more, or a turnover of one thousand crore rupees or more, or a net profit of five crore rupees or more. It must spend at least two per cent of its average net profits of the three preceding years. Limits can change by amendment.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: the least CSR spend
slides.body_md: The imagined Prithvi Cements had net profits of Rs 30 crore, Rs 45 crore and Rs 60 crore in the three preceding years. Find its least spend, as of 2024.
bullets: Step 1: Check that a limit is reached.
Step 2: Add the three profits and divide by three.
Step 3: Take two per cent of the average.

rows: Net profits of three years, Rs crore: 30, 45, 60
Latest net profit of Rs 60 crore is at least the Rs 5 crore limit

visual.alt: Worked example table: the imagined Prithvi Cements had net profits of 30, 45, 60 crore rupees, which sum to 135, an average of 45 crore, and two per cent of that is 0.9 crore rupees or 90 lakh rupees
visual.caption: Check coverage, then average, then two per cent.

slides.narration: The latest net profit is above five crore rupees, so the company is covered. The three profits add up to one hundred thirty five crore. Divided by three, the average is forty five crore. Two per cent of forty five crore is zero point nine crore rupees, which is ninety lakh rupees.

slides.heading: Quick check: the rule, as of 2024
slides.body_md: Fill in the blanks on the share of profit and the kind of profit.
slides.narration: Recall the percentage, and recall whether it is taken on a single year or on an average.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Obligation to act in line with the values of society; beyond legal duty
Eight arguments for; four against; each is a view, not a fact
Seven factors; section 135 sets a two per cent spend, as of 2024

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: concept, case for and against, kinds of responsibility, factors and the law

slides.narration: To sum up. Social responsibility is the obligation to act in line with the objectives and values of society, and it goes beyond legal duty. Eight arguments are put for it and four against, each as a view. There are four kinds. Seven factors led firms to accept it. And section one hundred thirty five sets a two per cent spend for covered companies, as of two thousand twenty four.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Give both sides, each as a view.
Add as of 2024 to the CSR rule.

rows: Treating social responsibility as the same as legal duty
Social responsibility goes beyond the law
Give both sides, each as the view of some people
Quoting the CSR rule with no date
Add as of 2024 and say the limits can change

visual.alt: Exam tips table: four common mistakes about social responsibility, a one-sided answer, an undated rule and real firm names

slides.narration: Some tips. Do not say that social responsibility and legal duty are the same. Present both the case for and the case against, using words such as some argue and others argue. Write as of two thousand twenty four next to the corporate social responsibility rule, and say that limits can change. And use made up firms in your examples.

visual.caption: Four groups and what is owed to each.

slides.narration: A business owes duties to four groups. To owners and shareholders, a fair return, safety of the investment and true information. To workers, fair wages, good working conditions and the right to form unions. To consumers, quality goods at fair prices, no adulteration, and handling of grievances. To the government and community, obeying laws, paying taxes honestly and protecting the environment.

slides.narration: Owners expect a fair return, the safety of their investment and true information about the firm. Workers expect fair wages, good working conditions and the right to form unions. Neglecting either group breaks a responsibility of the business, whether or not a law is also broken.

slides.narration: Consumers expect quality goods at fair prices, with no adulteration and no misleading advertisement, and they expect their complaints to be heard. The government expects obedience to laws and honest payment of taxes. The community expects the business to protect the environment and to help in its welfare.

slides.narration: Pollution is the release of harmful or unwanted substances or energy into the surroundings, making them less safe or fit for life. There are four kinds. Air pollution from smoke, dust and gases. Water pollution from waste in rivers and lakes. Land pollution from harmful solid waste. And noise pollution from loud and unwanted sound.

Weak checks and low concern for the environment

visual.alt: Table of causes of pollution from industry and their results: smoke and gases cause air pollution, untreated effluent causes water pollution, dumped waste causes land pollution, loud machines cause noise pollution, and out-of-date technology and weak checks add to all kinds

slides.narration: Smoke and gases from furnaces and boilers cause air pollution. Untreated effluent let into rivers causes water pollution. Waste dumped on open ground causes land pollution. Heavy machines cause noise. Out of date technology, no treatment of waste to save cost, and weak checks add to all kinds.

slides.heading: The need for pollution control

rows: Cleaner air and water keep workers and neighbours healthy
A firm that does no harm is less likely to face claims and penalties
Reuse of water and recovery of materials lower expense
People trust and prefer a firm that cares for the environment
Cleaner surroundings and a better life in the whole community

visual.alt: Table of five reasons for pollution control: reduced health hazards, reduced risk of liability, cost savings, improved public image and other social benefits

slides.narration: There are five reasons to control pollution. Reduced health hazards. Reduced risk of liability, since a firm that does no harm faces fewer claims. Cost savings, from reuse of water and materials. Improved public image. And other social benefits, such as a cleaner life for the whole community.

sections.heading: 1. Concept of social responsibility
sections.body_md:
**Social responsibility** is the obligation of business to take decisions and actions that are desirable in terms of the objectives and values of society.

**Legal responsibility** is the duty to comply with the law. Social responsibility goes beyond it: a firm may obey every rule and still fall short of what society values.

**Imagined example:** Rangrez Dyeworks sets up the wastewater unit that the rules demand (legal responsibility). If it also pays for a clean water tank for the villagers beside the river, it goes beyond the law.

sections.heading: 2. The case for and against social responsibility
sections.body_md:
**Some argue for it, on eight grounds:**
1. Justification for the existence and growth of business: it exists by the leave of society.
2. Long-term interest of the firm: a good name helps it to earn for years.
3. Avoidance of government regulation.
4. Maintenance of society: business depends on a sound society.
5. Availability of resources with business: money, skills and equipment.
6. Converting problems into opportunities.
7. A better environment for doing business.
8. Holding business responsible for the social problems it has caused.

**Others argue against it, on four grounds:**
1. Violation of the profit-maximisation objective.
2. Burden on consumers through higher prices.
3. Lack of social skills among managers.
4. Lack of broad public support.

Each point is a view held by some people. A balanced answer sets out both sides.

sections.heading: 3. Kinds of social responsibility
sections.body_md:
1. **Economic responsibility:** produce goods and services that society needs and earn a profit from them.
2. **Legal responsibility:** obey the laws of the land.
3. **Ethical responsibility,** including moral responsibility: do what is right and fair where no law compels it.
4. **Discretionary (voluntary) responsibility:** act or give by choice for society, with no law or custom demanding it.

**Imagined examples:** Tarang Appliances sells sound fans at fair prices (economic); Hariyali Paper Mills pays tax and keeps to smoke limits (legal); Amrit Dugdh will not sell a product it thinks unsafe (ethical); Byteloom Software lends staff to teach at a village school (discretionary).

sections.heading: 4. Factors behind social obligations; the law on CSR
sections.body_md:
**Factors that influenced the acceptance of social obligations:** the threat of public regulation; the pressure of the labour movement; the impact of consumer consciousness; the development of social standards; the development of business education; the relationship between social interest and business interest; and the development of a professional managerial class.

**Corporate social responsibility (CSR) under section 135 of the Companies Act 2013, as of 2024:** a company with a net worth of Rs 500 crore or more, or a turnover of Rs 1,000 crore or more, or a net profit of Rs 5 crore or more must spend at least 2 per cent of the average of its net profits of the three preceding years on CSR activities.

**Dated note, as of 2024:** limits and rules can change by amendment, so check the present position before relying on these figures.

**Worked check:** net profits of Rs 30, 45 and 60 crore have an average of Rs 45 crore, and 2 per cent of it is Rs 0.9 crore (Rs 90 lakh).

sections.body_md:
**Owners and shareholders:** a fair return, safety of the investment, and true information about the firm.

sections.heading: 6. Business and environmental protection
sections.body_md:
**Pollution** is the release of harmful or unwanted substances or energy into the surroundings, making them less safe or fit for life. Its **kinds** are air, water, land and noise pollution.

**Causes in industry:** smoke and gases; untreated effluent; dumped solid and chemical waste; loud machines; out-of-date technology and no waste treatment to save cost; weak checks and low concern.

**Need for pollution control:** reduced health hazards; reduced risk of liability; cost savings; improved public image; other social benefits.

**Role of business:** top management commitment; commitment throughout the enterprise; clear policies and programmes; compliance with laws; participation in government programmes; periodic assessment; and educating dealers and suppliers.

**Worked check:** recycling 10,000 litres a day at Rs 50 per 1,000 litres saves Rs 500 a day, or Rs 1,50,000 over 300 days.

sections.heading: 7. Business ethics
sections.body_md:
**Business ethics** are the socially determined moral principles that should govern business activities. Law is enforced by the state; ethics are the standards of right conduct that society holds.

**Elements:** top management commitment; publication of a code of conduct; establishment of compliance mechanisms; involving employees at all levels; and measuring results.

**Link with social responsibility:** ethics supply the moral base on which social responsibility rests, and social responsibility puts those principles into action for society. Ethical responsibility is also one of the four kinds of social responsibility.

**Worked check:** 34 of 40 breach reports settled is 85 per cent; an aim of 90 per cent needs 36, so 2 more.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Writing that social responsibility is the same as legal duty; it goes beyond the law.
- Giving only one side of the case; present both, each as the view of some people.
- Quoting the CSR rule without the words as of 2024, or without saying that limits can change.
- Listing stakeholders without saying what is owed to each.
- Naming the kinds of pollution without a cause or a reason for control.
- Mixing ethics with law; law is enforced by the state, ethics are held by society.
- Using real firms as examples; use made-up ones.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: a correct option or a quoted line from the case.
- 2 and 3 marks: one point per argument, kind, factor, duty or element, with a short explanation.
- 5 marks: five points, each with an explanation, in a numbered list.
- Case questions: quote the line, name the concept, explain in a sentence.

questions.stem_md: Which statement best describes the social responsibility of business?

options.text_md: The duty of a firm to maximise the wealth of its owners above everything else
The obligation of business to take decisions and actions that are desirable in terms of the objectives and values of society
The duty to obey the laws and to pay taxes, and nothing more
A sum that every firm must hand to the government each year

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The obligation of business to take decisions and actions that are desirable in terms of the objectives and values of society. Social responsibility looks to the objectives and values of society, so it reaches beyond profit and beyond bare legal compliance. Owner wealth alone is the profit view, obeying laws only is legal responsibility, and a fixed sum to the government is a tax.

questions.stem_md: Rangrez Dyeworks, an imagined dye factory in the imagined town of Rangpur, set up exactly the wastewater unit that the pollution rules demand and did nothing more. Its conduct meets its

options.text_md: legal responsibility, but not any voluntary one

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** legal responsibility, but not any voluntary one. Doing exactly what the law demands satisfies legal responsibility. Social responsibility goes beyond that, so the factory has not yet met any voluntary responsibility, and it cannot be said to have met none, since the law was followed.

questions.stem_md: Surya Steel Works, an imagined company, has engineers, trucks and cranes. Some people say it should lend them to rebuild a bridge washed away in a flood, because few other bodies in the district have such resources. Which argument for social responsibility is this?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Availability of resources with business. The point is that business holds the means that society needs, so it can help. Avoiding regulation is a different argument for, and the last two options are arguments against social responsibility.

questions.stem_md: Amrit Dugdh, an imagined dairy company, pays the farmers of the imagined village of Gokulpur a steady price. The farmers stay loyal and supply good milk for many years. Which argument for social responsibility does this support?

options.text_md: Holding business responsible for problems it has caused

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Long-term interest of the firm. Fair dealing built loyalty and a steady supply over the years, which serves the firm's own long-term interest. The second and third options are arguments against, and the fourth concerns harm that a firm has done.

questions.stem_md: The imagined association of leather makers of Charmpur adopted voluntary rules on waste disposal, so that the government need not frame stricter rules for them. Which argument for social responsibility does this reflect?

options.text_md: A better environment for doing business

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Avoidance of government regulation. Setting its own rules to keep the government from making tougher ones is avoidance of government regulation. The other options point to community conditions, the upkeep of society and fresh business openings, none of which the association mentions.

questions.stem_md: A shareholder of the imagined Dhara Foods says that every rupee spent on a free school for villagers is a rupee less for the owners. Which argument against social responsibility is this?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Violation of the profit-maximisation objective. The speaker sees social spending as cutting the profit meant for owners, which is the profit-maximisation argument. The other arguments against speak of prices and of skills, and the last option is an argument for.

questions.stem_md: A critic says that the cost of a new waste unit at the imagined Hariyali Paper Mills will be added to the price of its notebooks, and so the buyers will pay for it. Which argument against social responsibility is this?

options.text_md: Burden on consumers through higher prices

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Burden on consumers through higher prices. The critic fears that the cost will be passed on in higher prices, which is the burden on consumers. The others speak of public backing, of managers' skills and of owner profit.

questions.stem_md: Some argue that the managers of the imagined Tarang Appliances are trained to make and sell fans, not to run health camps or village schools, so they may run such work poorly. This is the argument of

options.text_md: justification for the existence of business

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** lack of social skills. The point is that business managers may not have the skills that social work needs. The second and third options speak of profit and price, and the last is an argument in favour.

questions.stem_md: Tarang Appliances, an imagined firm, makes sound ceiling fans, sells them at fair prices and earns a profit from doing so. Which kind of social responsibility is this?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Economic responsibility. Producing goods that society needs and earning a fair profit is the economic responsibility. Legal responsibility is about following laws, ethical about doing what is right, and discretionary about voluntary acts.

questions.stem_md: Hariyali Paper Mills, an imagined firm, files its returns on time, pays its taxes and keeps to the limits on factory smoke. Which kind of social responsibility does this show?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Legal responsibility. Keeping to the law of the land is legal responsibility. Discretionary acts are voluntary, economic responsibility concerns production and profit, and ethical responsibility concerns doing right where the law is silent.

questions.stem_md: No law bans a certain cheap sweetener, but the imagined Amrit Dugdh will not use it in its sweets because it believes that the sweetener could harm children. Which kind of social responsibility is this?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Ethical responsibility. The firm avoids something it holds to be wrong although no law forbids it, which is ethical responsibility, including moral responsibility. A legal duty would follow a rule, an economic one concerns trade, and a discretionary act is a free giving to society, not a refusal to do harm.

questions.stem_md: Byteloom Software, an imagined firm, lets its staff take paid days to teach computer skills at a village school. No law or custom requires this. Which kind of social responsibility is this?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Discretionary responsibility. An act of giving that the firm chooses freely is discretionary, or voluntary, responsibility. Legal responsibility would be required by law, and economic responsibility concerns production and profit. Nothing in the scene suggests a breach of ethics.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined town of Lohanagar, workers of several mills formed unions and pressed their employers for safe machines and fair hours, and the mills began to treat workers better. Which factor behind the acceptance of social obligations is this?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Pressure of the labour movement. Workers organising and pressing for better conditions is the pressure of the labour movement. The scene mentions no new law, no school of management and no action by buyers.

questions.stem_md: Surya Steel Works, an imagined company covered by section 135 of the Companies Act 2013, made net profits of Rs 60 crore, Rs 75 crore and Rs 90 crore in the three preceding years. As of 2024, the least it must spend on corporate social responsibility in the year is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Rs 1.5 crore. The average of the three years is Rs 75 crore, and 2 per cent of it is Rs 1.5 crore. Rs 0.75 crore is one per cent of the average, Rs 3 crore is 4 per cent, and Rs 75 crore is the average itself.

questions.stem_md: As of 2024, Dhara Foods, an imagined company, has a net worth of Rs 150 crore, a turnover of Rs 600 crore and a net profit of Rs 4 crore in the preceding year. Is it bound by the corporate social responsibility spending rule of section 135 of the Companies Act 2013?

options.text_md: Yes, because its turnover is above Rs 500 crore
No, because it is below all three limits
Yes, because every company must spend on corporate social responsibility
Yes, because it earns some profit

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** No, because it is below all three limits. The limits are a net worth of Rs 500 crore, a turnover of Rs 1,000 crore and a net profit of Rs 5 crore; the firm reaches none of them. The figure Rs 500 crore applies to net worth, not to turnover, and the duty is not on every company or on every profitable one.

questions.stem_md: The managers of the imagined Hariyali Paper Mills showed a loss in the year as a profit in the report sent to shareholders. Which responsibility towards owners did they fail?

options.text_md: Giving true information about the firm

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Giving true information about the firm. Reporting a loss as a profit misleads the owners, so it breaks the duty of true information. Wages and consumer grievances concern other groups, and the scene does not mention any labour law.

questions.stem_md: The owner of the imagined Lohanagar Cycle Works sacks any worker who talks of forming a union. Which responsibility towards workers does he neglect?

options.text_md: Respecting the right to form unions

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Respecting the right to form unions. Workers may form unions to speak for themselves, and punishing them for it violates that right. The other options concern owners, the government and consumers.

questions.stem_md: Nirmal Masala, an imagined spice seller, is found mixing coloured sawdust into chilli powder. Which responsibility towards consumers is broken?

options.text_md: The right of workers to unionise

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** No adulteration of goods. Mixing a cheap foreign material into a product is adulteration, which a business must avoid. The other options concern workers, owners and the government.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Kanak Jewellers keeps two sets of account books so that it can show a lower profit and pay a smaller tax. Which responsibility towards the government does it fail?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Paying taxes honestly. Hiding profit to cut tax goes against honest payment of taxes, a duty to the government. The other options concern consumers, workers and dealers.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Rangrez Dyeworks lets untreated coloured water run into the imagined river Nirmala, and fish in the river die. Which kind of pollution is this?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Water pollution. Untreated waste released into a river harms the water, so it is water pollution. Air pollution concerns smoke or gases, land pollution concerns waste left on the ground, and noise pollution concerns loud sound.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Charmpur Tannery dumps heaps of chemical sludge on an empty plot behind its factory, and nothing will grow there. Which kind of pollution is this?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Land pollution. Harmful solid waste left on the ground that spoils the soil is land pollution. The scene says nothing about a river, a sound or a gas.

questions.stem_md: Residents beside the imagined Lohanagar Press Shop cannot sleep because the heavy machines run loudly through the night. Which kind of pollution does this show?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Noise pollution. Loud, unwanted sound from machines is noise pollution. The other kinds concern the ground, water and air.

questions.stem_md: After Rangrez Dyeworks recycled most of its water, its monthly water bill fell sharply. Which reason for pollution control does this show?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Cost savings. A smaller bill is a saving in cost. Image, liability and health are other reasons for controlling pollution, but the scene mentions none of them.

questions.stem_md: The board of the imagined Hariyali Paper Mills approves a written environment policy, sets aside a budget for it and the chief executive speaks about it at every meeting. Which step in controlling pollution is this?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Top management commitment. A board and chief executive backing the cause with policy and money show commitment from the top. The other options concern outside parties, review and public schemes.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Tarang Appliances holds workshops for its dealers and suppliers on how to dispose of packing waste safely. Which step in controlling pollution is this?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Educating dealers and suppliers. Teaching those who trade with the firm to handle waste properly is educating dealers and suppliers. The other options concern law, commitment from the top, and review.

questions.stem_md: Which statement best describes business ethics?

options.text_md: The rules of the government on taxes and licences
The socially determined moral principles that should govern business activities
The profit that a firm earns in a year
The private beliefs of each owner, which society cannot judge

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The socially determined moral principles that should govern business activities. Ethics are moral principles set by society to guide conduct in business. Rules on taxes and licences are law, profit is a result and not a principle, and ethics are judged by society, not only by the owner.

questions.stem_md: Byteloom Software, an imagined firm, puts a written code on its website that says how its people must treat clients, colleagues and data. Which element of business ethics is this?

options.text_md: Publication of a code of conduct

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Publication of a code of conduct. A written statement of conduct made public is the publication of a code of conduct. Measuring results, compliance mechanisms and involving employees are the other elements, and the scene shows none of them.

questions.stem_md: Byteloom Software sets up an ethics committee and a private helpline on which an employee may report a breach without fear. This is the element of
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** establishing compliance mechanisms. A committee and a helpline are the means by which the code is enforced, so they are compliance mechanisms. The code itself is only the statement of conduct.

questions.stem_md: At the end of each year, Byteloom Software counts the breaches reported, the cases settled and the staff who completed ethics training, and compares them with last year. Which element of business ethics is this?

options.text_md: Publication of a code of conduct

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Measuring results. Counting and comparing outcomes year on year is measuring results. The other elements concern the stand of the leaders, the written code and the part played by staff.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Nirmal Masala asks its packers, drivers and clerks, along with its managers, to help write its rules of conduct and to attend sessions on them. Which element of business ethics is this?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Involving employees at all levels. Asking staff at every level to take part is involving employees at all levels. The scene does not describe the leaders' stand, a count of outcomes, or a committee.

questions.stem_md: Which statement best relates business ethics to social responsibility?

options.text_md: Ethics matter only to firms that are too small to have any social responsibility
Ethics supply the moral principles on which a firm's social responsibility rests
Social responsibility is a kind of law, while ethics have no link to society
The two are opposed, so a firm must choose one

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Ethics supply the moral principles on which a firm's social responsibility rests. Moral principles guide what a firm sees as right towards society, so ethics form the base of its social responsibility. Size has no bearing, social responsibility is wider than law, and the two support one another.

questions.stem_md:

**Reason (R):** Social responsibility asks for decisions and actions that fit the values of society, and that can go beyond what the law demands.

Choose the correct option.

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true. Because social responsibility reaches beyond the law, legal compliance alone may fall short of it, so R explains A.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true. Lasting loyalty and goodwill are the way in which fair dealing pays the firm, so R explains A.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true: the base is the average net profit of the preceding three years. R is false, because turnover is only one of the tests of coverage and is not the base of the amount.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Business ethics are rules that only the government can write and enforce.

**Reason (R):** Business ethics are moral principles that society works out to guide business conduct.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A is false: ethics are set by society, and a firm can follow them even where there is no law. R is true, since ethics are socially determined moral principles.

**Assertion (A):** Controlling pollution can lower the costs of a factory.

**Reason (R):** A factory that recycles water or recovers waste materials buys less of them afresh.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true. Reusing water or materials cuts what the factory must buy, which is how pollution control saves money, so R explains A.

questions.stem_md: Social responsibility of business means the same thing as obeying the law.
questions.solution_md: **False.** Legal responsibility is only one part of it. Social responsibility also asks a firm to act in line with the values of society where the law is silent.

questions.stem_md: Discretionary responsibility is voluntary: a firm takes it up by choice and no law requires it.
questions.solution_md: **True.** Discretionary or voluntary acts are done by choice, which marks them off from legal and economic duties.

questions.stem_md: Loud and unwanted sound from factory machines is counted as a kind of pollution.
questions.solution_md: **True.** Noise pollution is one of the four kinds, with air, water and land pollution.

questions.stem_md: A firm that has published a fine code of conduct has done all that business ethics ask of it, even if nobody checks whether the code is followed.
questions.solution_md: **False.** A code is one element. Without compliance mechanisms, training and a count of results, it may remain words on paper.

questions.stem_md: Moral responsibility is counted within the ethical kind of social responsibility.
questions.solution_md: **True.** The ethical kind of responsibility includes moral duty, which is doing right and fair even where no law demands it.

questions.stem_md: As of 2024, a company covered by section 135 of the Companies Act 2013 must spend at least ___ per cent of its average net ___ of the three preceding years on corporate social responsibility.
questions.solution_md: The minimum is 2 per cent of the average net profits of the preceding three years.

questions.stem_md: Untreated factory effluent released into a river causes ___ pollution, while loud machinery causes ___ pollution.
questions.solution_md: Effluent in a river is water pollution; loud machinery is noise pollution.

questions.stem_md: Business ethics are the socially determined ___ principles that should ___ business activities.
questions.solution_md: Ethics are moral principles that govern business activities.

questions.stem_md: Match each act of an imagined firm with the kind of social responsibility that it shows.

options.text_md: Tarang Appliances sells sound fans at fair prices and earns a profit
Hariyali Paper Mills pays its taxes and keeps within the legal smoke limits
Amrit Dugdh refuses to sell a product it thinks unsafe, though no law bans it
Byteloom Software lends its staff to teach at a village school

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). Production and profit are economic; following the law is legal; doing what is right without a legal push is ethical; a free act of giving is discretionary.

questions.stem_md: Match each duty of the imagined Hariyali Paper Mills with the group to which it is owed.

options.text_md: Paying a fair return and giving true information
Safe working conditions and the right to form unions
Handling complaints about goods and avoiding misleading advertisements
Paying taxes honestly and caring for the town's environment

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(q), (b)–(s), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). A return and true information are owed to owners; conditions and unions to workers; complaints and honest advertising to consumers; taxes and environment to the government and the community.

questions.stem_md: Arrange the steps by which an imagined company finds out its minimum corporate social responsibility spend, as of 2024.

options.text_md: Take 2 per cent of the average as the minimum spend
Add the net profits of the three preceding years
Divide the sum by three to get the average
Check that net worth, turnover or net profit reaches the set limit

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (d) → (b) → (c) → (a). First confirm that the company is covered, then add the profits, find the average, and take 2 per cent of it.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: Arrange these steps by which an imagined software firm builds an ethical workplace, in a sensible order.

options.text_md: A code of conduct is written and published
The number of breaches and cases settled is counted each year
Staff at every level are trained in the code
An ethics committee and a helpline are set up
The leaders announce that ethics come before targets

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (e) → (a) → (d) → (c) → (b). Leaders set the stand, the code is published, the means of enforcing it are set up, staff are trained, and finally the results are measured.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: Define the social responsibility of business and state one way in which it differs from legal responsibility.
questions.solution_md: Meaning and one difference.

answer.model_answer_md: Social responsibility is the duty of a business to act and decide in ways that society, by its goals and values, regards as desirable. It differs from legal responsibility, which only asks that the firm obey the law, because it goes beyond it.

questions.stem_md: The owner of the imagined Dhara Foods says that a free eye camp for the village would eat into the profit of the firm. Name the argument and explain it in one sentence.
questions.solution_md: Argument named and explained.

answer.model_answer_md: This is the argument of violation of the profit-maximisation objective. Some argue that a firm exists to earn the highest profit for its owners, so money spent on camps and other social work reduces what the owners should receive.

questions.stem_md: Explain how avoidance of government regulation is argued as a reason for a business to be socially responsible.
questions.solution_md: The argument and how it works.

answer.model_answer_md: Some argue that when firms act responsibly by themselves, the government has little reason to frame strict rules for them. A firm that cares for society keeps its freedom to run its affairs, and so a response to the people's needs may keep new regulation away.

marking_scheme.step: Responsible conduct leaves less reason for regulation
Firm keeps its freedom of action

questions.stem_md: State any two factors that have led businesses to accept social obligations, with a few words on each.
questions.solution_md: Any two factors.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Threat of public regulation: firms act on their own so that the government is not forced to make rules.
2. Impact of consumer consciousness: buyers who know their rights expect fair goods and honest dealing, and firms respond.

questions.stem_md: State any two responsibilities of a business towards its consumers.
questions.solution_md: Any two responsibilities.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. It must supply goods of good quality at fair prices, free from adulteration.
2. It must not mislead buyers by false advertisements, and it must listen to their complaints and settle them promptly.

questions.stem_md: Lohanagar Cycle Works pays below what the work deserves and keeps its welding shop poorly ventilated. Which responsibilities towards workers does it neglect? Name two.
questions.solution_md: Two responsibilities with the case.

answer.model_answer_md: It neglects the duty to pay fair wages, since pay is below what the work deserves, and the duty to provide good working conditions, since the welding shop is badly ventilated and may harm the health of its workers.

questions.stem_md: What is meant by pollution? Name any two kinds of pollution.
questions.solution_md: Meaning and two kinds.

answer.model_answer_md: Pollution is the release of harmful or unwanted substances or energy into the surroundings, so that air, water or land becomes unsafe or unfit for life. Two kinds are air pollution and water pollution; land and noise pollution are others.

questions.stem_md: Rangrez Dyeworks cleans its wastewater and avoids a heavy claim for damage from the villagers of Rangpur. Which two reasons for pollution control does this show? Explain briefly.
questions.solution_md: Two reasons with explanation.

answer.model_answer_md: It shows the reduced risk of liability, since the firm is no longer likely to face a claim for harm done to the villagers. It also shows reduced health hazards, since cleaner water protects the people of Rangpur from illness.

questions.stem_md: Why is the commitment of top management called the first step in controlling pollution in a business?
questions.solution_md: Why the top matters.

answer.model_answer_md: Because policy, money and attention for the cause come from the top. If the board and senior managers are firmly behind it, the staff will treat pollution control as a priority, and without that backing the other steps are unlikely to be taken.

marking_scheme.step: Policy and resources come from the top
Staff follow the lead of top managers

questions.stem_md: Define business ethics and give one imagined example of an ethical act.
questions.solution_md: Meaning and an example.

answer.model_answer_md: Business ethics means the moral principles, shaped by society, that ought to guide what a firm does. For example, the imagined Nirmal Masala may recall a batch of its spice that fails a quality test, though no one has yet complained.

questions.stem_md: Why does a firm publish a code of conduct as part of its ethics programme?
questions.solution_md: Two reasons.

answer.model_answer_md: A published code tells employees, customers and others what behaviour the firm expects and will not accept. Because it is open to everyone, the firm can be held to it, and workers know clearly what is right and wrong in daily work.

marking_scheme.step: Makes the firm answerable to the public

questions.stem_md: Explain any three arguments that are put forward in favour of social responsibility of business.
questions.solution_md: Any three arguments.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Long-term interest: a firm with a good name and loyal partners earns for years.
2. Maintenance of society: business depends on society, so it benefits from a healthy one.
3. Availability of resources: business holds money, skills and equipment that social work needs. Other arguments are avoiding regulation and a better environment for business.

questions.stem_md: Some argue that business should not take up social responsibility. Explain any three of their arguments.
questions.solution_md: Any three arguments, stated as views of those who hold them.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Violation of profit maximisation: some argue that a firm exists to earn the highest profit, and social spending cuts it.
2. Burden on consumers: the cost may be added to prices.
3. Lack of social skills: managers are trained for business, not for social work. Lack of broad public support is another view.

questions.stem_md: Explain any three kinds of social responsibility of business.
questions.solution_md: Any three kinds.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Economic: producing goods and services that society needs and earning a profit from them.
2. Legal: obeying the laws of the land, such as paying taxes.
3. Ethical: doing what is right and fair, including moral duty, where the law does not compel it. Discretionary responsibility, a voluntary giving to society, is the fourth.

questions.stem_md: Explain any three factors that have helped to bring about the acceptance of social obligations by business.
questions.solution_md: Any three factors.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Pressure of the labour movement: organised workers demanded fair treatment.
2. Development of social standards: society came to expect honest and fair conduct.
3. Development of a professional managerial class: trained managers see their duty to society as well as to owners. Threat of regulation and consumer consciousness are others.

questions.stem_md: As of 2024, explain the main features of the corporate social responsibility spending rule in section 135 of the Companies Act 2013.
questions.solution_md: Coverage, amount and purpose.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. It binds a company with a net worth of Rs 500 crore or more, a turnover of Rs 1,000 crore or more, or a net profit of Rs 5 crore or more.
2. Such a company must spend at least 2 per cent of the average of its net profits in the three preceding years.
3. The money goes to corporate social responsibility activities.

marking_scheme.step: Limits that bring a company under the rule
Two per cent of the average net profit of three years

questions.stem_md: Explain the responsibilities of a business towards its owners and shareholders.
questions.solution_md: Three responsibilities.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. A fair return: the firm should try to give the investors an adequate share of its earnings.
2. Safety of the investment: the capital that they put in should not be put at risk through reckless decisions.
3. True information: accounts and reports must show the real position, without hiding losses.

questions.stem_md: Explain any three reasons why a business needs to control pollution.
questions.solution_md: Any three reasons.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Reduced health hazards: cleaner air and water keep workers and neighbours healthy.
2. Cost savings: reusing water and materials lowers expenses.
3. Improved public image: people trust and prefer a firm that cares for the environment. Lower risk of liability and other social benefits are further reasons.

questions.stem_md: Explain any three elements of business ethics.
questions.solution_md: Any three elements.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Top management commitment: leaders show by word and deed that they stand for ethical conduct.
2. Publication of a code of conduct: a written statement tells everyone what is expected.
3. Compliance mechanisms: a committee or helpline sees that the code is followed. Involving employees and measuring results are the other two.

questions.stem_md: Explain any five arguments given in favour of social responsibility of business.
questions.solution_md: Five arguments, each with a line of reasoning.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Justification for existence: business exists to serve society, so it should answer to it.
2. Long-term interest: goodwill and loyal customers help a firm earn for many years.
3. Avoidance of government regulation: responsible conduct leaves less reason for strict rules.
4. Availability of resources: business has the money, skills and equipment that social work needs.
5. Holding business responsible for problems it has caused: a firm that pollutes should help to repair the damage.

questions.stem_md: Explain the kinds of social responsibility, with an imagined example of each kind.
questions.solution_md: Four kinds with examples and a closing point.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Economic: producing needed goods and earning a profit, as Tarang Appliances does with sound fans.
2. Legal: obeying the law, as Hariyali Paper Mills does when it pays tax and keeps to smoke limits.
3. Ethical: doing right where no law compels, as when Amrit Dugdh will not sell a product it thinks unsafe.
4. Discretionary: giving voluntarily, as when Byteloom Software lends staff to a village school.
5. Together they run from what society needs of business to what business may choose to give.

questions.stem_md: Some argue for and others against the social responsibility of business. State two arguments on each side and say which side seems stronger to you for a firm that pollutes a river, with a reason.
questions.solution_md: Two arguments for, two against, and a reasoned view.

answer.model_answer_md:
For: 1. Long-term interest, as goodwill brings lasting custom. 2. Holding business responsible for harm it causes.
Against: 1. Violation of profit maximisation, as social spending cuts owner profit. 2. Burden on consumers, as the cost may be added to prices.
View: for a firm that pollutes a river, the arguments in favour look stronger, because the harm is its own doing and the cost of repair should not fall on the villagers.

marking_scheme.step: Side chosen for the polluting firm

questions.stem_md: Explain the responsibilities of a business towards workers, consumers and the government and community.
questions.solution_md: Responsibilities to the three groups.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Workers are owed a fair wage, a sound workplace and freedom to organise in a union.
2. Workers also need respect and a safe workplace, so that they can work without fear.
3. Consumers: goods of good quality at fair prices, with no adulteration or misleading advertisements.
4. Consumers also need their complaints to be heard and settled quickly.
5. Government and community: obeying laws, paying taxes honestly, protecting the environment and helping the welfare of the community.

marking_scheme.step: Consumers: quality, prices, no adulteration or false advertising

questions.stem_md: Explain any five steps that a business can take to control pollution.
questions.solution_md: Five steps with a line each.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Top management commitment: the board backs the cause with a policy and funds.
2. Commitment throughout the enterprise: every department and worker is brought into the effort.
3. Clear policies and programmes: the aims and the steps are written down.
4. Compliance with laws: the firm keeps within the limits set for emissions and waste.
5. Periodic assessment of progress, with educating dealers and suppliers and joining government programmes as further steps.

questions.stem_md: Explain the elements of business ethics, with an imagined software firm as the example.
questions.solution_md: Five elements with the example.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Top management commitment: the chief of Byteloom Software states that ethics come before targets.
2. Publication of a code of conduct: the firm posts a written code on its website.
3. Compliance mechanisms: an ethics committee and a private helpline see that the code is followed.
4. Involving employees at all levels: every worker, from intern to manager, is trained and asked for views.
5. Measuring results: the firm counts breaches reported and cases settled each year.

questions.stem_md: Read the passage and answer the questions that follow. *(Imagined factory, river and town.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** **Correct option: (a)** water pollution. Coloured wastewater in a river spoils the water, so it is water pollution. The other kinds concern sound, air and the ground.

**(b)** The line on the fishers and the children.

**(c) (i)** Litres saved, daily value and yearly saving.

**OR (c) (ii)** Payback period and the reason.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (a) water pollution

**(b)** "**The fishers of Rangpur caught fewer fish and many children on the bank developed skin rashes**": this is harm to the livelihood and health of the community.
